We closed the quarter at ninety-four per cent of plan.
Since April we have been carrying a heavier weather load than we modelled.
Two of the largest losses were reported after the cut-off, so they sit in this quarter and not in the last one.
What changed the number was not frequency. It was severity.
The three accounts that drive most of the variance are all in the same region.
We should have flagged the concentration in February, and I take that.
On the evidence we have, the trend would appear to hold into Q4, though I would not commit to a number today.
Denise, thank you for the half hour. This is not an appraisal. I do one of these at the midpoint of every senior development plan, and mostly I am listening.
Understood. Then let me take stock properly, rather than tell you it is going well.
That already puts you ahead of most of the plans on my desk. Start wherever the evidence is.

In January the quarterly read-out was drafted for me and I delivered it as written. In June I gave it live, I took eleven minutes of questions, and the meeting did not move into Portuguese. What changed was not the vocabulary. It was the structure.
And the part that has not moved?

Written work. I have been drafting the same regional directive three times since March, and the third version is the one that gets circulated. That is the plateau. It should have been flagged by me in the first quarter, and it was not.
It was flagged. Not by you — Milan raised it in April. That is not a criticism. It is why I asked for this conversation.

Then the second half is a consolidation, not an expansion. On the evidence we have, the spoken side is holding under pressure and the writing is where the step change has to come from. One demonstrable milestone for December, rather than four soft ones.
Send me the one, in writing, by Friday. And Denise — the reason I take these seriously is that most people at your level describe a feeling. You have just given me a trajectory.
Rather than tell you it is going well, let me take stock.
What changed was not the vocabulary. It was the structure.
It should have been flagged by me, and it was not.
That is the plateau, and I would rather name it myself.
One demonstrable milestone by December, not four soft ones.

Most people arrive at a midpoint review with a feeling and a list. The feeling is that it is going well, and the list is how much they have done. Neither of those is evidence, and I have stopped asking for them. What I count is narrower. Name a situation you could not handle at the start, tell me when you handled it, and tell me who was in the room. One of those is worth more to me than a whole term of activity. The second thing I would say is about plateaus. Almost everybody is on one at the halfway mark, and it is not a failure. It is what learning looks like once the easy gains are gone. The mistake people make there is to add something new, when what is half-built is the thing that needs to be made solid. The second half of any plan is not for learning more. It is for making what already exists hold under pressure.

For about four months in the middle of it, I improved in nothing. I was working as hard as I ever had, and all of that work was going into the parts that were already automatic. That is what a plateau actually is. It is not laziness. It is effort landing in the wrong place. I had assumed the problem was that I needed more words. The words were there. What I was not doing was using them anywhere uncomfortable. The inflection point was not a course and it was not a book. It was being asked to chair a call I had attended silently for two years. I was worse at it than I wanted to be, and the following month I was measurably better. One last thing, and it is the practical one. Keep a short record of what you handled, with dates on it. You forget very quickly what you could not do six months ago, and when somebody asks you for evidence, a feeling is not going to help you.

Rather than tell you it is going well, let me take stock of where this actually stands. In June I gave the read-out live and took eleven minutes of questions. Written work has not moved since March, and that is the plateau. So the second half consolidates, and I will set one demonstrable milestone for December.
